cards.explanation: The answer is their fellow Jews. Verse 1 says the outcry is "…against their fellow Jews." The people crying out are pointing at their own people, and that's a hard thing to cry out about. Nehemiah, the governor of Judah, is about to hear every bit of it.

The answer is their fields and homes. Verse 3 says, "We are mortgaging our fields, our vineyards, and our homes to get grain during the famine." Think about that, friends. They're putting up the very ground they stand on just to get food. That's a heavy price for a basket of grain.

The answer is True. Verse 3 says they are mortgaging their fields, vineyards and homes "…to get grain during the famine." Verse 2 says they need grain to eat and stay alive. Hungry families and a lot of pressure.

The answer is "others." Some of the people say in verse 5 that they are powerless to redeem their daughters "…because our fields and vineyards belong to others." The land is no longer theirs, and they can't redeem their daughters. I think that's a painful spot for any parent to stand in.

The answer is False. Nehemiah, the governor of Judah, says in verse 6, "When I heard their outcry and these complaints, I became extremely angry…" He doesn't stay calm and quiet. Then, after serious thought, he rebukes the nobles and officials.

The answer is that they're charging interest to their own brothers. Nehemiah says, "You are exacting usury from your own brothers!" (Nehemiah 5:7). Usury is charging extra on what people borrow. And he says it about their own brothers.
The answer is False. Verse 8 says, "But they remained silent, for they could find nothing to say." They don't argue and they don't make excuses. I think that kind of silence says plenty.

The answer is mockery from their foreign enemies. Nehemiah asks, "Shouldn’t you walk in the fear of our God to avoid the reproach of our foreign enemies?" (Nehemiah 5:9). Reproach means the sneering and shame that outsiders throw at you. He's saying how they live affects how the nations around them see them.

The word is "immediately." Nehemiah says, "Please restore to them immediately their fields, vineyards, olive groves, and houses, along with the percentage of the money, grain, new wine, and oil that you have been assessing them." (Nehemiah 5:11) No "let me get back to you." He wants it all restored immediately.

The answer is the percentage they've been charging. Nehemiah asks them to restore the land "…along with the percentage of the money, grain, new wine, and oil that you have been assessing them." (Nehemiah 5:11). It's not just the property, friends. He wants back the extra they've been charging, too.

The answer is False. The nobles and officials reply, "We will restore it…" and say they "…will require nothing more from them. We will do as you say." (Nehemiah 5:12). Their reply is a yes, and it says nothing about needing time.

The answer is "priests." Nehemiah tells it this way in verse 12: "So I summoned the priests and required of the nobles and officials an oath that they would do what they had promised." The priests are the ones he summons. The oath is required of the nobles and officials.

The answer is to shake him out of his house. Nehemiah says, "May God likewise shake out of his house and possessions every man who does not keep this promise." (Nehemiah 5:13). He's shaking out his robe as he says it, so the picture goes with the words. It's a serious way to say the promise is serious.

The answer is that they do as they promised. Verse 13 ends, "And the people did as they had promised." Plenty of folks make big promises, and this crowd actually followed through. That's the best part of the whole scene, bakers.

The number is twelve. Nehemiah says in verse 14, "…from his twentieth year until his thirty-second year (twelve years total)…" That's the time he serves as governor, from the year King Artaxerxes appointed him. Twelve years is a long stretch.

The answer is the food allotted to the governor. Nehemiah tells us in verse 14, "…neither I nor my brothers ate the food allotted to the governor." That food was allotted to the governor, and he and his brothers didn't eat it for those twelve years. The text goes on to say why in verse 15.

The answer is their servants. Verse 15 says, "Their servants also oppressed the people." So the weight on the people came from the governors and from the people working for them. Then Nehemiah says, "But I did not do this, because of my fear of God."

The answer is False. Nehemiah says in verse 16, "…I devoted myself to the construction of the wall, and all my servants were gathered there for the work; we did not acquire any land." His time went to the wall, and no land was acquired.

The answer is True. Nehemiah tells us in verse 17, "There were 150 Jews and officials at my table, besides the guests from the surrounding nations." That's a full house, friends. I've had six cookie cutter kids at my counter and I thought THAT was crowded.

The answer is that the people's burden is so heavy. Verse 18 says, "But I did not demand the food allotted to the governor, because the burden on the people was so heavy." He could have claimed it, and he chose not to. That tells you where his heart was.

The answer is to remember him favorably. Nehemiah prays, "Remember me favorably, O my God, for all that I have done for this people." (Nehemiah 5:19). He takes it straight to God. A short prayer like that tells me a lot.
